skill.name: finishing-a-development-branch
skill.description: Guides a completed development branch through test verification, merge, pull request creation, preservation, or discard decisions.
skill.summary: Completes development branches with structured test, merge, PR, and cleanup decisions.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: Most static hits are Markdown fence false positives, but several workflow steps do run external git, test, and GitHub CLI commands. Confirmed risks are legitimate branch-completion actions with repository state impact, plus a contradictory worktree cleanup path that could remove a worktree after creating a pull request. No evidence found of prompt injection, credential exfiltration, or hidden network behavior beyond the documented GitHub CLI workflow.

remediation.issue: Project test commands can execute code from the current branch.
remediation.suggestion: Warn users before running package scripts or tests in untrusted repositories and ask for approval when trust is unclear.

remediation.issue: Merge, push, branch deletion, and worktree removal change repository state.
remediation.suggestion: Keep explicit user selection and require approval before push, branch deletion, or worktree removal.

remediation.issue: The pull request workflow conflicts with later worktree cleanup guidance.
remediation.suggestion: Make Option 2 consistent by preserving the worktree or asking for separate cleanup confirmation.

remediation.issue: The worktree detection command uses unquoted command substitution.
remediation.suggestion: Quote the branch name output and use fixed-string matching, or replace the pipeline with a structured git query.

static_findings.snippet: git merge-base HEAD main 2>/dev/null || git merge-base HEAD master 2>/dev/null

finding_verdicts.reason: The span instructs running npm test, cargo test, pytest, or go test. Project tests can execute repository code and package scripts, so this is real external command execution.
This span is a Markdown code fence closing marker and text introducing failed tests. It does not contain an executable command or unsafe interpolation.
The block is example output for failing tests, not a shell command. It tells the agent to stop when tests fail.
This span contains Markdown fence closure and process prose before base branch detection. No executable command is present in this finding.
The command is a hardcoded read-only git merge-base lookup with no user-controlled shell interpolation. It only discovers the base branch and suppresses stderr.
This span closes the base-branch command block and introduces the option menu. It contains no executable command.
The cited block is a user-facing menu template. It lists choices and does not execute commands or access files.
This span contains menu closure and headings for the next process step. I found no executable instruction in the cited evidence.
The merge workflow includes git checkout, git pull, git merge, a test command, and branch deletion. These legitimate steps change repository state and run external commands.
This span closes the merge command block and introduces the pull request option. The actual push and PR commands start at line 91.
The pull request workflow pushes a branch to origin and runs gh pr create. These commands change remote repository state and invoke the GitHub CLI.
This span contains Markdown closure and descriptive text for keeping or discarding work. It does not include an executable command.
The cited block is a confirmation prompt that lists what will be deleted. It does not execute deletion by itself.
This span requires exact user confirmation and opens the next command block. No executable command appears before line 129.
The discard workflow runs git branch -D after checkout, which force-deletes a local branch. It is guarded by confirmation but remains destructive external command execution.
This span is Markdown closure and worktree cleanup prose before the check command. It does not execute anything by itself.
The command invokes git and grep with unquoted command substitution from the current branch name. It is read-only, but shell word splitting can make the check unreliable for unusual branch names.
This span closes the worktree check block and introduces conditional text. It contains no command to execute.
git worktree remove deletes the local worktree path when cleanup is selected. It is intended cleanup, but it can remove local files and working context.
The substitution uses a single-quoted heredoc passed to cat to build pull request text, so it does not evaluate body content as shell. The remote PR side effect is covered by the line 91 finding.
The grep command uses unquoted output from git branch --show-current. This does not show arbitrary command execution, but it can cause unsafe argument parsing or incorrect matches.
The cited PR command block performs git push and gh pr create, and includes shell substitution to construct the PR body. It is legitimate but changes remote repository state.
The cited worktree check uses command substitution inside a shell pipeline. The command is read-only, but unquoted branch output can be parsed as unintended grep arguments.
The evidence is stderr redirection to /dev/null during a read-only git lookup. It does not read user files, write project data, or exfiltrate information.

semantic_findings.title: Contradictory Worktree Cleanup Instructions
semantic_findings.description: The pull request path sends the agent to cleanup, while later reference sections say Option 2 should keep the worktree. This contradiction can cause unintended worktree removal after creating a pull request.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The cited lines give directly conflicting guidance about whether the pull request option keeps or removes the worktree. The risk is operational data loss or user surprise, not hidden malicious intent.

content.value_statement: Completed branches still need careful integration choices, test checks, and cleanup. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code through structured merge, pull request, keep, or discard decisions.
actual_capabilities: Requires passing tests before presenting integration options.
Helps identify the base branch with git merge-base or user confirmation.
Presents four explicit choices: local merge, pull request, keep branch, or discard work.
Guides local merge, push, pull request creation, and worktree cleanup steps.
Requires typed confirmation before discarding branch work.
Lists common mistakes and red flags for final branch handling.
limitations: It assumes a git repository with a feature branch workflow.
It does not choose an integration path without user selection.
Pull request creation depends on GitHub CLI access.
Approved actions can change local or remote repository state.

use_cases.title: Finish a Feature Branch
use_cases.description: Verify tests, choose a merge path, and complete a local branch without open-ended follow-up.

use_cases.title: Prepare a Pull Request
use_cases.description: Push completed branch work and prepare a pull request with a summary and test plan.

use_cases.title: Clean Up Development Worktrees
use_cases.description: Remove branches or worktrees only after tests pass and the user confirms the chosen outcome.

prompt_templates.title: Finish My Branch
prompt_templates.prompt: Finish my current development branch. Verify tests first, then present the four completion options and wait for my choice.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Pull Request
prompt_templates.prompt: My implementation is complete. Help me push this branch and create a pull request with a clear summary and test plan.
prompt_templates.scenario: Opening a pull request for review

prompt_templates.title: Merge Locally
prompt_templates.prompt: Guide me through merging this completed branch back to the base branch locally. Re-run tests after the merge before cleanup.

prompt_templates.title: Assess Completion Risk
prompt_templates.prompt: Audit the completion path for this branch. Verify tests, determine the base branch, compare merge versus pull request, and handle cleanup only after approval.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced workflow with repository state risk

output_examples.input: Finish this branch after implementation is complete.
output: Tests passed. Implementation is ready for a completion choice.
Options: merge locally, push and create a pull request, keep the branch, or discard the work.
Waiting for your selected option before changing repository state.

output_examples.input: Create a pull request for this completed branch.
output: The branch is ready to push after test verification.
The pull request draft will include a concise summary and test plan.
Cleanup will wait for your explicit approval.
The discard path requires typed confirmation before deletion.
The response will list the branch, commits, and worktree path affected.
No branch or worktree removal happens until confirmation is exact.

best_practices: Run the relevant project tests before selecting a completion path.
Confirm the base branch before merging or deleting branch work.
Use typed confirmation for destructive discard and cleanup actions.
anti_patterns: Merging or opening a pull request while tests are failing.
Deleting a branch or worktree without confirming what will be removed.
Using open-ended prompts when a structured completion choice is needed.

faq.question: Does this skill run tests?
faq.answer: It guides test verification before integration choices. The exact command depends on the project.

faq.question: Can it merge a branch locally?
faq.answer: Yes. It can guide checkout, update, merge, test verification, and branch cleanup after approval.

faq.question: Can it create pull requests?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes a GitHub CLI pull request path when repository access is available.

faq.question: Does it delete work automatically?
faq.answer: It requires a selected completion path. The discard path requires exact typed confirmation before branch deletion.

faq.question: Does it support git worktrees?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes worktree cleanup guidance for selected completion paths.

faq.question: Which tools support it?
faq.answer: The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.
